title: A Grave in the Promised Land
summary: Sarah dies at Hebron at the age of 127, and Abraham mourns her. Needing a place to bury her, he negotiates in public with the Hittites of the city and with Ephron, who owns the cave of Machpelah. After a courteous and carefully witnessed exchange, Abraham pays four hundred shekels of silver, and the field and its cave become his legal property, where he buries Sarah.
story: Sarah, the mother of the promise, has seen Isaac born and grown. Now she dies, and her death forces a question the story has carried since Genesis 12: God promised Abraham the land, but after some sixty years he still owns none of it, except the rights to a well at Beersheba (Genesis 21:30). This chapter records his first real purchase of land in Canaan, and it is a grave. The patriarchs will be buried here one by one (Genesis 25:9; 49:29-32; 50:13), and the promise will stay unfulfilled in their lifetimes. The chapter is a quiet act of faith: Abraham buries his wife in the land God promised, as if the promise were already true.
historical:
Hebron, also called Kiriath-arba, lies in the hill country about thirty kilometers (roughly twenty miles) south of Jerusalem, near the oaks of Mamre where Abraham had long camped. The traditional site of the cave of Machpelah is in Hebron, enclosed by a massive stone wall built in the Herodian period, around the turn of the eras; the structure, known as the Tomb of the Patriarchs, is still revered by Jews and Muslims.

The Hittites of this chapter, called the sons of Heth, are puzzling. The best-known Hittites ruled an empire in Anatolia (modern Turkey) from their capital Hattusa in the second millennium BC, far to the north. Genesis 10:15 lists Heth among the descendants of Canaan, and many scholars think the Hittites at Hebron were a local group with a similar name, or a small population connected with the north; others think the name was applied loosely to earlier inhabitants. The legal form of the purchase has been compared with Hittite law (by Manfred Lehmann in 1953) and with later Mesopotamian sale documents (by Gene Tucker in 1966). The comparisons are suggestive, but neither pins down a date.
cultural:
Abraham calls himself “a foreigner and an outsider” (verse 4), a resident alien who could graze flocks but had no right to own land. Buying property required the consent of the community, which is why the negotiation happens publicly at the city gate, before “all the Hittites who had come to the gate of his city” (verse 10), who serve as witnesses. The exchange follows Near Eastern courtesy. Ephron offers the field as a gift; this was a polite opening, and accepting it would have left Abraham's claim open to challenge later. Abraham insists on paying “full price” (verse 9), so that the land is unmistakably his.

Silver was weighed, not counted, since coins came centuries later; “according to the standard of the merchants” (verse 16) refers to accepted commercial weights. Four hundred shekels is a large sum, perhaps around four and a half kilograms of silver. For comparison, Jeremiah later bought a field for seventeen shekels (Jeremiah 32:9), and many commentators think Ephron's modest-sounding “what is that between you and me?” named a high price. The deed lists the field, the cave, and all the trees within its boundaries, as land contracts of the period often did.
literary: The chapter is framed by Sarah's death (verses 1-2) and her burial (verses 19-20), with a long negotiation in between, told in three rounds of speech: Abraham and the Hittites (verses 3-6), Abraham and the Hittites about Ephron (verses 7-11), and Abraham and Ephron (verses 12-16). The phrase “bury my dead” or “bury your dead” recurs throughout like a refrain. So do the words for hearing and presence, since the whole transaction depends on public witness. The legal completion is spelled out twice (verses 17-18 and 20), with the key word possession, which ties this purchase to God's promise of the land “as an eternal possession” (Genesis 17:8). Sarah is the only woman in Genesis whose age at death is recorded.

outline.t: Abraham asks the Hittites for a burial site
Negotiations with Ephron for the cave of Machpelah
The field is deeded, and Sarah is buried

doctrines.note: Abraham buries Sarah in the land God promised but has not yet given. The grave is a claim on the future. Hebrews 11:13 says the patriarchs died in faith, without having received what was promised, seeing it and welcoming it from afar.
Faith takes ordinary, legal, practical form here. Abraham doesn't wait passively for God to hand over the land; he buys the first piece of it, honestly and publicly, trusting the rest to God.
Abraham, the man of faith, mourns and weeps for Sarah (verse 2). Grief is not a failure of faith. Scripture gives mourning its place and its time before the practical business of burial goes on.

words.note: Ger, a sojourner or resident alien: someone living among a people not his own, without the rights of a native. Abraham names himself this way. Israel's law later commands care for the ger, reminding Israel that they too were strangers in Egypt (Exodus 22:21), and 1 Peter 2:11 calls Christians sojourners and exiles in the world.

Achuzzah, possession, especially landed property held by right. God had promised the land “as an eternal possession” (Genesis 17:8). Here the word appears for Abraham's first legally held piece of it, a burial plot, a small down payment on the whole.

Nasi, a leader or prince, someone lifted up. The Hittites call Abraham a nasi of God, rendered “God's chosen one” in the BSB and elsewhere as a mighty prince, since God's name can also function in Hebrew to mark something as very great. Either way, the locals regard Abraham with respect as a powerful figure among them.

christ: Jesus appeals to the patriarchs buried in this cave when he answers those who denied the resurrection. God said to Moses, long after Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had died, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” and Jesus draws the conclusion that God is not the God of the dead but of the living (Matthew 22:31-32). The grave at Machpelah, then, is not the end of the promise. Hebrews 11:9-16 reads Abraham's life as a stranger in the promised land as a sign that he was looking for “the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God,” and says God is not ashamed to be called their God. Christians confess that Christ's own bodily resurrection is the firstfruits of the hope in which Abraham laid Sarah in the ground.

hard.q: Why does Stephen say in Acts 7:16 that Abraham bought a tomb at Shechem from the sons of Hamor?
hard.a:
Genesis 23 says Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah at Hebron from Ephron the Hittite. Genesis 33:19 says Jacob bought land at Shechem from the sons of Hamor, and Joshua 24:32 says Joseph's bones were buried there. Stephen's speech in Acts 7:16 seems to combine these, speaking of a tomb Abraham bought from the sons of Hamor at Shechem.

Interpreters respond in several ways. Many see a deliberate compression: Stephen is summarizing Israel's history rapidly and telescopes two patriarchal purchases and two burial places into one sentence. Some propose that Abraham, who built an altar at Shechem (Genesis 12:6-7), may also have acquired land there, though Genesis doesn't record it. Others hold that Luke accurately reports what Stephen said, including a slip in a speech given under pressure, without endorsing every detail. On any of these readings, the Genesis account of Machpelah stands, and Stephen's point, that the patriarchs died owning only graves in a land still promised, is the same point Genesis 23 makes.

questions: Abraham grieved openly before he took care of business. How do you and your community make room for grief?
Abraham called himself a foreigner in the land God had promised him. In what ways do Christians still live as sojourners?
Abraham's first piece of the promised land was a grave. What does it mean to act on a promise you will not see fulfilled in your lifetime?
